summary:
Venezuela does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct: the age of consent is 16 and applies identically to same-sex relations, and homosexuality is legal. The country has no hate-crime statute and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, so conduct directed at trans people attracts no dedicated penalty. Visitors should note that legality on paper has not prevented police action: in May 2026 NGOs including the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state, where officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality'.

There is no working legal gender recognition route. A 2017 constitutional action filed before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be assessed individually against certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist certifying the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal has still not granted the requested name and gender changes. Identity documents are equally blocked: SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people may request an identity card matching their gender identity, but no administrative procedure or mechanism exists to enact the relevant article, leaving trans visitors and residents without a document that reflects their gender.

Conditions have deteriorated alongside the political crisis. The Washington Blade reported on 10 September 2024 that LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution following the disputed July 2024 election, with the persecution tied directly to the political upheaval; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 September 2024. The European Union Asylum Agency maintains a dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of Venezuela within its country-focus material covering the reference period through 2025, used in international protection decisions, and AFS and the Vance Center published an LGBTQ guide on Venezuela in October 2024.

The statute book offers trans and LGB visitors little protection elsewhere as well. The law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, although lesbian couples are permitted to access IVF, and an equal-marriage bill was slated for introduction to the National Assembly in January 2014 with no later enactment recorded.
tangentialFactors:
Openly LGBT political figures have been targeted by the state. Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla, a Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian, a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell, as reported by El Mundo on 13 December 2015. Tamara Adrián, the country's first transgender candidate, stood for the National Assembly in August 2015, and both she and Mantilla were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of the legislature.

Official recognition of LGBT dates has been contested internally. Venezuela has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and in May 2016 the National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia; the Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016. The government has recently begun participating in Pride events.

Public opinion data point in a more permissive direction than the legal framework. A Cronica Uno poll of 2–3 March 2023 found a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens, with 82% familiar with the LGBTIQ+ term and 13% not; 36% regarded gay, lesbian or bisexual orientation as innate. A 2023 Equilibrium CenDE poll found 48% of Venezuelans supported adoption by same-sex couples, 34% totally and 14% somewhat, against 39% opposed. A 2013 Pew survey recorded 57% of 18–29-year-olds saying homosexuality should be accepted by society, compared with 51% of 30–49-year-olds and 45% of those over 50.

A legislative push for equal marriage was reported by Aporrea on 31 January 2014, when a bill was to be presented to the National Assembly that week; no later enactment is recorded.
localsOnly:
Trans Venezuelans seeking legal recognition must litigate case by case through a 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal, producing certified birth certificates and a specialist psychiatric and psychological report on the veracity of the intended sexual identity. The Tribunal has not granted the requested name and gender changes. The September 2016 SAIME announcement that a new identity card matching gender identity may be requested has no procedure behind it, so identity-card information remains unchanged in practice.

Transition care has no footing in statute: the law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions. Reproductive access is split by orientation, with lesbian couples allowed IVF while same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. On 15 December 2016 the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ruled that a baby may be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames, basing the decision on Article 75 of the Constitution and declaring that the state must protect all families without distinction, so that children and teenagers born into same-sex families enjoy all the rights and guarantees of children born into opposite-sex families.

The universal age of consent is 16, with no differential age for same-sex conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border-document rules for trans travellers, including whether a passport or entry record may carry a gender marker that differs from presentation, or whether immigration screening risks disclosure. That layer remains unsourced here.

Whether the Supreme Justice Tribunal has granted any name or gender change since the 2017 constitutional action was filed is not resolved; the available material records only that none has been granted.

There is no reported outcome, prosecution or disciplinary follow-up for the May 2026 police raid in Barquisimeto, Lara state, beyond the NGOs' denunciation. The independence of the officers' conduct and any accountability measures are not documented in this inventory.

The status of the January 2014 equal-marriage bill after its reported introduction is unresolved, as is whether any anti-discrimination or hate-crime measure has been tabled since. Public-opinion figures cited are dated to 2013, 2023 and 2023 respectively and are not current.
